subject: Banking
title: Insurance and Cross-Selling
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Insurance and Cross-Selling.

hook.text: Banks sell insurance, investments, and credit monitoring alongside checking accounts.

buildup.text: Wells Fargo's strategy was '8 products per household.' Push every customer toward credit cards, mortgages.

discovery.text: Cross-selling works because trust in a checking account makes customers more open to higher-margin add-ons.

twist.text: Wells Fargo opened 3.5 million fake accounts to meet cross-selling targets.

climax.text: Cross-selling is profitable when ethical. But aggressive targets turn bankers into salespeople, customers into quotas.

punchline.text: 8 products per customer. Wells Fargo faked 3.5 million accounts to meet it.

quiz.question: What did Wells Fargo do to meet cross-selling targets?

details.summary: Banks generate significant fee revenue by cross-selling insurance, investment products, and protection plans to their existing customer base. This one-stop-shop strategy leverages the trust relationship to sell increasingly more products per customer.
details.whyItMatters: Cross-selling tactics can blur the line between helpful advice and aggressive product pushing. The Wells Fargo fake accounts scandal was the extreme result of cross-selling pressure taken to illegal extremes.
takeaways: The average profitable bank customer holds three to five products
Cross-selling insurance and investments generates higher margins than basic banking
Wells Fargo's cross-selling scandal revealed the dangers of aggressive targets

faq.question: Why do banks push so many products on customers?
faq.answer: Each additional product increases revenue per customer and reduces the likelihood of them switching banks. A customer with a checking account, credit card, mortgage, and insurance is deeply embedded and far more profitable than a single-product customer.

faq.question: Is cross-selling bad for consumers?
faq.answer: It depends on execution. Genuinely useful product recommendations benefit customers. But aggressive sales targets, as seen at Wells Fargo, can push employees to sell unnecessary products or even create fraudulent accounts to meet quotas.
